newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Aerospatiale swings back to profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Aerospatiale swings back to profit.

text.p: French state-owned Aerospatiale reported on Friday a return to profit for 1996, with a recovery in civilian aircraft markets allowing it to avoid restructuring charges which had previously tipped it into loss.

The group, due to merge with combat plane maker Dassault Aviation this year and be privatised, posted a net profit after payment to minority shareholders of 812 million francs ($140 million). That compares with a prior-year loss of 981 million, which included 1.4 billion in restructuring charges.
The company issued a bullish 1997 forecast. "The results for the 1997 year should...see a very significant turn in the group's profitability, allowing a doubling of profits," it said in a statement.
Aerospatiale makes parts and assembles passenger jets for the Airbus Industrie consortium, and also manufactures tactical and strategic missiles, satellites and helicopters.

Sales this year are expected to hit 60 billion francs, versus 50.9 billion, helped by increased aircraft sales to Airbus, cost-cutting measures and the rise in the dollar. It expects to deliver 190 Airbus jets, up from 126 in 1996.

"The major difference between 1995 and 1996 comes basically from the fact we had high restructuring charges in 1995. The recovery in business means we do not need new provisions in 1996," chairman Yves Michot told a news conference.

Aerospatiale reported operating profit up 15 percent at 736 million francs versus 639 million a year ago. Its share in the Airbus consortium provided by far the biggest operating profit contribution, with 1.175 billion francs, versus 1.075 billion.
Aerospatiale owns 38 percent of Airbus, alongside Daimler-Benz Aerospace (Dasa). British Aerospace Plc (BAe) owns 20 percent, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain holds four percent.

The helicopter business, held through a 70 percent stake in the Eurocopter joint venture with Dasa, dented Aerospatiale's results to the tune of 224 million francs, but was lower than the 817 million franc hit taken in 1995.
After a 1996 loss expected to be around 300 million, Eurocopter's prospects should improve with 11.8 billion francs of new orders booked last year versus 6.8 billion in 1995.
Space and defence activities contributed 206 million francs to operating profit, down from 412 million.
Other aeronautical activities ran a loss of 314 million francs, versus a 156 million loss in 1995, mainly due to a mediocre market in aircraft maintenance.
New orders surged to 63.3 billion francs compared with 39.3 billion in 1995. The total order book stood at 129.9 billion francs last year versus 101.2 billion.
Net debt, which fell by 3.6 billion francs to 2.9 billion, was made up mainly by late payment by the state, finance director Francois Auque said.
Its debt should be practically nil by 1998, Michot said.
The planned merger with Dassault should result in an increase in equity capital, which was considered to be insufficient at the current 4.9 billion francs.
Michot said he hoped privatisation of the merged group could take place by November or December, if market conditions allow.
He added that there were no differences of opinion with Dassault over the privatisation, which he hoped would follow the example of French computer maker Bull.
The state privatised Cie des Machines Bull by opening up its capital rather than a stockmarket flotation.
Michot reiterated that all major French and European players were welcome to take a stake in Aerospatiale and he mentioned Dasa, BAe and General Electric Co Plc. ($ = 5.777 French Francs)
